profile.reading:
This building is Equinix's SV1 facility, part of Equinix's Silicon Valley data center network in the San Jose/Santa Clara area. Equinix was founded in 1998 by Al Avery and Jay Adelson, both former Digital Equipment Corporation facilities managers, on the idea of building a neutral place where competing internet networks could physically connect and exchange traffic, a model that let the company grow through network effects as more networks joined; Equinix converted to a real estate investment trust in January 2015 and trades on Nasdaq as EQIX. Silicon Valley, where Equinix is still headquartered today in nearby Redwood City, was the company's founding market, and its San Jose facilities on Great Oaks Boulevard and its Santa Clara facilities on Corvin Drive and Duane Avenue grew into one of the densest interconnection hubs in Equinix's global network as the company expanded internationally, entering Asia-Pacific in 2002, Europe via the IXEurope acquisition in 2007, Latin America in 2011, and the Middle East in 2013, and opening its 50th global data center in London by 2010 around the time it acquired Switch and Data Facilities Company. Equinix's own published specifications for the flagship SV1 building on this campus describe an 82,850-square-foot, single-story, steel-frame facility with N+1 power redundancy, a minimum cabinet density of 2kVA, 120v/208v power distribution, and generators rated for 30 hours or more at full load; Equinix markets the Great Oaks campus for its direct connections to major networks and tier-1 cloud service providers. Equinix's website did not disclose this specific building's own square footage or power capacity separately from the SV1 figure cited as representative of the broader campus.

Pacific Gas and Electric, the regional utility serving most of Silicon Valley, and Silicon Valley Power, Santa Clara's municipal utility, have both cited sustained data center load growth across the San Jose-Santa Clara-Sunnyvale corridor in their own capacity planning, a dynamic distinct from the newer data center markets elsewhere in the country given how built-out and power-constrained the Bay Area grid already is after decades of continuous data center development since Equinix's own 1998 founding in the area.

reading.body:
SV1 is a 82,850 sq ft facility in San Jose operated by Equinix as part of a 12-building Silicon Valley metro cluster serving over 10,500 customers. The operator publishes no megawatt capacity figure for this building, making its power envelope opaque to public assessment. N+1 power redundancy and N+2 cooling redundancy qualify it for mission-critical colocation workloads that cannot tolerate downtime.

Without published power capacity, SV1's potential to host AI compute cannot be directly assessed. The facility is one of 103 mapped data centers in California but ranks outside the top 11 by published megawatts, indicating either smaller capacity than disclosed peers or deliberate non-disclosure. In a state holding 365 MW of published data center capacity, this building's actual contribution to AI infrastructure remains unknown.

The absence of a power specification from Equinix's own page for a retail colocation facility suggests either that capacity is allocated per-tenant under service agreements rather than published in aggregate, or that SV1 operates within broader campus power budgets not broken out by building. For readers evaluating where AI scaling can expand in Silicon Valley, SV1 cannot be ranked against other sites without that figure.
